background.definition: A ganglion cyst is a cystic collection of synovial fluid within a joint or tendon sheath that usually develops spontaneously in adults between the ages of 20 and 50 years.

list.listitem: Ganglia are the most common soft-tissue tumor of the hand and wrist.
Female to male preponderance of ganglia is 3:1.
Causes of most wrist ganglia are unknown.
Cystic structures are often near or attached to tendon sheaths and joint capsules.
More common in women, young people (20s to 50s), and in persons with previous cyst.
Cyst may be due to herniation of synovial lining creating a "one-way valve."
Cyst may be due to benign tumor growth.
Stress or microtrauma causing stimulation of the cyst may contribute to its growth.
Typically presents as a gradually enlarging cyst or nodule on the palmar or dorsal aspect of the wrist. C
Aspiration of jelly-like fluid confirms a ganglion cyst. C
Ultrasound or MRI should be ordered in conjunction with orthopedic consult in patients with abnormal presentations. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath

Differential.Differential_Features: Puncture wound, stab wound, or laceration
Normal response to a nerve transection, common in amputations

list.listitem: Typical history includes an enlarging cyst over several months that likely started after trauma or repetitive microtrauma.
Patients may report weakness or altered range of motion of the wrist. Radiation of pain into the forearm is not unusual, perhaps due to associated tendinopathy.
Palmar wrist ganglions usually present as swellings on the palmar radial aspect of the wrist, adjacent to the radial artery.
Dorsal wrist ganglions classically present over the scapholunate interval.
Examination reveals a firm, usually nontender cyst that feels like a small marble under the skin and transilluminates with a penlight.
Atypical presentation should prompt referral to specialist with or without imaging or diagnostic aspiration.
No diagnostic tests are needed with a typical presentation.
Radiographs are rarely, if ever, helpful in evaluation of ganglion cyst.
MRI or ultrasound may be helpful in narrowing the differential with atypical presentations, such as wrist pain of unknown etiology, and in assessing the anatomy of the wrist.
Typical ultrasound findings reveal a discrete hypoechoic mass without internal vascularity but with posterior acoustic enhancement.
Aspiration of jelly-like fluid confirms the diagnosis.
Patients initially present with a nodule on the dorsal or palmar wrist.
If a ganglion is confidently suspected based on history and physical expression, reassure patient that the process is benign and no treatment is necessary.
If the nodule is causing discomfort, inhibiting normal function, or is of cosmetic concern, consider aspiration.
Aspiration of jelly-like fluid confirms a ganglion cyst.
If the history, physical expression, or aspiration is atypical, consider further workup, including imaging studies (MRI or ultrasound) or referral to a specialist.
Reassurance and observation alone is a reasonable first choice, since 40% to 53% of cysts resolve spontaneously without treatment. C

Aspiration temporarily eliminates the cyst but has a high recurrence rate (59%) and may be no better than reassurance. Surgical excision is a more definitive therapy and has a low recurrence rate (5%-21)%).B
Aspiration followed by steroid injection or aspiration with cyst puncture is no more effective than aspiration alone. B
Because one-third to one-half of cysts resolve spontaneously, consider reassurance and pain control with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents.

Clinic aspiration under local anesthesia is often performed as an initial therapy prior to surgical excision, but has not been well studied. A systematic review identified one cohort study that found no significant difference in outcomes between aspiration and reassurance. The same systematic review found a 59% recurrence rate in published case series of aspiration.

Begin with a 25-gauge needle on a 3-cc syringe to inject 1% lidocaine to the overlying skin for anesthesia. Aspirate the fluid using a 16-gauge needle with a 10-cc syringe. Be sure to completely evacuate the fluid by using the opposite hand to milk the tumor. A large-bore needle is usually required because of the viscous nature of the fluid.
Aspiration followed by steroid injection or aspiration with cyst puncture is no more effective than aspiration alone.
Repeated aspiration at the same site increases the risk of joint contamination and secondary sepsis.
Surgery has a much lower recurrence rate (5%-20%) and is the definitive therapy. Arthroscopic surgery may be an option for both dorsal and volar wrist ganglia.

A systematic review of interventions for dorsal wrist ganglion cysts only found 5 RCTs (N = 233) and deemed the quality of evidence low. The recurrence rates were 7-72% for aspiration (with or without injection of an additive), 6-41% for open excision, and 0-16% for arthroscopic resection.
Rupture by digital pressure or with a swift blow is unnecessarily traumatic and has little chance of long-term success.
Referral to a hand surgeon is indicated for persistent or recurrent pain, recurrent cyst, or cosmetic deformity.
Surgical resection of a palmar ganglion cyst requires mobilization and protection of the radial artery.
Approximately one-third to one-half of wrist ganglions resolve spontaneously. B
Surgery has a success rate of 73% to 99%. B
Cysts located at the dorsum of the distal interphalangeal joint and nail base, often called mucous cysts, are associated with a secondary nail deformity in the elderly population.

In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, another type of dorsal wrist ganglion often appears that is easily differentiated by its soft, irregular appearance and association with proliferative rheumatoid extensor tenosynovitis.
